issues.subcategory: Incorrect serial mediation calculation
issues.description: Hypothesis 4 specifies a serial indirect effect from experienced patient incivility to enacted incivility through negative emotions and compassion fatigue. A serial indirect effect should multiply all component paths in the chain (experienced incivility → negative emotions; negative emotions → compassion fatigue; compassion fatigue → enacted incivility), i.e., a × d × b or equivalent. The manuscript states it was estimated by multiplying only the first and last stages “a × d,” which is the same notation used for the two-path mediation in Hypothesis 2. This is mathematically inconsistent with the hypothesized three-link serial mediation and makes the reported indirect effect difficult to interpret and potentially wrong.
issues.quote: Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d).

issues.subcategory: Indirect effect value inconsistent with reported path coefficients
issues.description: The reported serial indirect effect for Hypothesis 4 is inconsistent with the regression coefficients in Table 2. Using the reported paths T2 customer incivility → T3 negative emotions (B=.26), T3 negative emotions → T4 compassion fatigue (B=.37), and T4 compassion fatigue → T4 enacted incivility (B=.57), the serial indirect effect would be approximately .26 × .37 × .57 = .055. This approximates the reported .06 only if all three paths are multiplied, contradicting the manuscript’s statement that only a × d was used. If only .26 × .37 is used, the effect would be .096, not .06. This creates uncertainty about what was actually estimated.
issues.quote: T2 Customer Incivility ... .26*** ... T3 Negative Emotions ... .37*** ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .57*** ... Customer Incivility  Negative Emotions  Compassion Fatigue  Enacted Incivility | .06** | .02 | 2.58

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent standard error for indirect effect
issues.description: The text reports the Hypothesis 4 indirect effect as B=.06, SE=.04, p<.01, 95% CI [.02, .10], whereas Table 2 reports B=.06, SE=.02, t=2.58. A standard error of .04 would imply a test statistic around 1.5, not p<.01, and would generally be inconsistent with the stated confidence interval. This suggests a reporting or computational error.
issues.quote: Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]).

issues.subcategory: Relative importance analysis impossible as described
issues.description: The relative importance analysis claims that three predictors accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively. These percentages sum to 100%, implying they are proportions of explained variance, not total variance. However, the text says each predictor accounted for that percentage of the variance, which is misleading. In addition, the predictors are highly collinear, so relative importance estimates are sensitive to method choice and should be interpreted cautiously; no confidence intervals are reported.
issues.quote: The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.subcategory: Relative importance coefficients contradict preceding regression coefficients
issues.description: The supplemental lm() regression reports negative emotions and compassion fatigue both as B=.23, SE=.04, p<.001, whereas Table 2 reports negative emotions B=.28, SE=.10 and compassion fatigue B=.57, SE=.17 for the enacted incivility equation. The text also states compassion fatigue has a parameter estimate nearly six times that of negative emotions, which conflicts with both Table 2 (.57 vs .28, about two times) and the subsequent lm() regression (.23 vs .23, equal). These inconsistencies undermine confidence in the analyses.
issues.quote: As seen in Table 2, the last step of the simple mediation reflects a parameter estimate for compassion fatigue that is nearly six times that of negative emotions. ... we regressed enacted incivility on predictors from this stage--experienced incivility (B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40), negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001), and compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001).

issues.subcategory: Table 3 contains malformed or duplicated columns and impossible entries
issues.description: Table 3 is not interpretable as reported. Column headers are duplicated and misaligned, several cells appear repeated, and some coefficients lack standard errors or significance markers while being discussed as significant. For example, the table displays multiple duplicate B columns and reports R2 as “.” for one model. This prevents verification of moderated regression results.

issues.subcategory: CFA test statistic missing and model factors inconsistent
issues.description: The CFA result omits the chi-square symbol and reports only “(269)=862.05.” More importantly, the text says a four-factor model was tested, yet the study includes at least five substantive constructs in the hypothesized model: experienced incivility, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, enacted incivility, and patient acuity. If patient acuity was excluded because it is a single item, this should be explicitly stated. The CFA as reported does not establish discriminant validity for all hypothesized constructs.
issues.quote: First, we assessed our hypothesized four-factor model absent of the temporal control measures. ... The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99)

issues.subcategory: Questionable CFA fit interpretation
issues.description: The manuscript characterizes RMSEA=.08 as acceptable while chi-square is large, but provides no SRMR, factor loadings, residuals, factor correlations, or comparison model statistics. Given the very high correlations among constructs (e.g., T3 negative emotions, T4 compassion fatigue, and T4 enacted incivility correlations up to .96), discriminant validity is a major concern and requires fuller reporting.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors.

issues.subcategory: Extreme multicollinearity among predictors and constructs
issues.description: The correlations among key constructs are extremely high, including T3 negative emotions with T4 compassion fatigue (r=.96) and T4 enacted incivility with T4 compassion fatigue (r=.91). These values suggest possible construct redundancy, common-method inflation, or response-pattern artifacts. Regression and mediation estimates with such collinearity may be unstable and difficult to interpret, yet no VIFs, latent variable approach, or robustness checks are reported.
issues.quote: T3 Negative Emotions ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .96 ... T4 Enacted Incivility ... .94 | .91

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent sample sizes across methods, results, and tables
issues.description: The final sample is reported as N=372, but Table 1 and Table 2 use N=321, and Table 3 uses N=244 due to missingness on the moderator. The loss from 372 to 321 is not explained, nor is the missing-data mechanism evaluated. This is a substantial discrepancy affecting power, representativeness, and interpretation.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.subcategory: Table sample size conflicts with final sample
issues.description: The manuscript states that the final analytic sample was N=372 after excluding incomplete and low-quality cases, but the main correlation and mediation tables report N=321. The manuscript does not explain why 51 additional participants were omitted from the main hypothesized model.
issues.quote: Note. N = 321. Cronbach’s α presented on the diagonal.

issues.subcategory: Large unhandled missingness on moderator
issues.description: The moderated analysis uses N=244, meaning 128 of the final N=372 or 77 of the N=321 table sample were lost because of missing patient acuity. The manuscript notes missingness but does not report the amount clearly in the methods, test whether missingness is random, compare included versus excluded cases for moderation analyses, or use principled missing-data methods such as FIML or multiple imputation.
issues.quote: Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.subcategory: Listwise deletion despite nontrivial missing data
issues.description: The authors appear to use complete-case/listwise deletion for missing patient acuity and perhaps other variables. Given that 55% of acuity missingness was due to nonresponse and 45% to out-of-range answers, missingness could plausibly relate to workload, acuity, comprehension, or data quality. Complete-case analysis may bias moderation estimates and reduce power.
issues.quote: Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response).

issues.subcategory: Dropout design creates nonrandom attrition risk
issues.description: Participants who missed one wave were not invited to subsequent waves, which converts temporary nonresponse into permanent attrition. This design can induce bias if missingness is related to workload, fatigue, incivility, shift scheduling, or patient acuity. The manuscript provides only a limited comparison of T1-only participants and completers and does not evaluate those excluded for data quality or missed later waves in detail.
issues.quote: Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys (i.e., a participant who did not complete T2 survey was not sent the link for the T3 or T4 surveys).

issues.subcategory: Incomplete reporting of exclusions
issues.description: The stated exclusions do not add up transparently. Starting with 468 at T1, 450 responded at T4, but the final sample is 372 after excluding 16 for missing time points and 78 for poor data quality. Yet 468 - 16 - 78 = 374, not 372. The data quality categories also list n=56 inconsistent demographics and n=1 excessive missingness, leaving 21 of the 78 poor-quality exclusions unexplained.
issues.quote: Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample. Responses were considered failed data quality checks if they had any of the following characteristics: (a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age); or (b) missing values exceeded 50% of the questions (n = 1). This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.subcategory: Nonprobability convenience and social media recruitment
issues.description: Recruitment relied on flyers, personal networks, and social media/forum postings. This self-selected convenience sample may overrepresent nurses interested in incivility, those with particular work experiences, or those active online. The sampling frame and response rate are unknown, limiting representativeness and generalizability.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies. First, we dropped off recruitment flyers... Second, we sent emails to nurses and other healthcare professionals in our personal networks... Finally, we posted study information and recruitment materials online via personal social network accounts...

issues.subcategory: Inclusion criteria inconsistently stated
issues.description: The recruitment materials specify full-time nurses in high-stakes/critical care settings, but the final sample description says all participants were employed as nurses part- or full-time and worked more than one shift per week. This inconsistency changes the target population and could affect workload, exposure, and acuity estimates.
issues.quote: Information about inclusion criteria (working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse) and compensation were also provided along with the link to participate.

issues.subcategory: Full-time criterion contradicted by final sample description
issues.description: The methods state the inclusion criterion was full-time nursing, but later reports inclusion of part-time nurses. This contradiction makes it unclear who was eligible and whether eligibility was enforced.
issues.quote: All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time), worked more than one shift a week, on average, and routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients.

issues.subcategory: Eligibility verification insufficient
issues.description: The authors relied on highlighting the nursing focus and directly asking participants if they met criteria. No verification of employment, role, unit type, licensure, or shift patterns is reported. Given online/social media recruitment and monetary incentives, misclassification or fraudulent participation is a concern, especially because many were excluded for inconsistent demographics.
issues.quote: To help ensure that the participants were from healthcare contexts, we highlighted the nursing focus in the recruitment and consent information and directly asked participants if they met the inclusion criteria.

issues.subcategory: Self-report single-source design for all substantive variables
issues.description: All predictors, mediators, moderators, and outcomes were self-reported by the same respondents. This is particularly problematic for enacted incivility, a socially undesirable behavior, and for patient acuity, which could be objectively measured. Temporal separation helps but does not eliminate common method bias, social desirability, negative affectivity, or response-style effects.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.subcategory: No control for baseline levels of mediators/outcomes in reported regressions
issues.description: Although T1 controls are referenced in Table 1, the reported regression models do not appear to control for prior levels of the dependent variables (e.g., T1/T2 negative emotions, compassion fatigue, enacted incivility). Without autoregressive controls, the analyses cannot distinguish change over time from stable between-person differences. This weakens claims that experienced incivility predicts future increases in emotions, fatigue, or enacted incivility.
issues.quote: We tested this hypothesis by regressing negative emotions toward patients (T3) onto experienced patient incivility (T2).

issues.subcategory: Repeated weekly measures not modeled as panel or multilevel data
issues.description: The study collected all constructs at all four waves, but the main analyses use selected time points rather than exploiting the full longitudinal panel. The approach does not model within-person change, autoregression, random intercepts, reciprocal effects, or nesting of repeated observations within individuals. This limits the ability to claim temporal unfolding and may confound stable individual differences with longitudinal effects.
issues.quote: To better understand the effect of the predictor variables on the criterion variable at the subsequent time point, we assessed each variable during each wave. This allowed us to assess the covariances between all variables (including controls) within each wave... The subsequent waves were included for hypothesis testing

issues.subcategory: Causal claims from observational panel mediation
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly uses causal language such as “leads to,” “drives,” “impact,” and “exacerbates” despite an observational self-report design without randomization, experimental manipulation, or adequate control for confounding and baseline outcomes. Temporal ordering alone does not establish causality, especially given possible reverse causation and stable negative affectivity.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.

issues.subcategory: Unaddressed confounding by trait negative affectivity and response style
issues.description: Negative affectivity, neuroticism, burnout proneness, social desirability, job stress, unit culture, shift type, and workload could influence reports of experienced incivility, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility. The manuscript does not control for these factors, making the proposed mediation vulnerable to omitted-variable bias.
issues.quote: Our results support a partial mediation process: in support of our hypotheses, experiencing incivility from patients was related to increased future incivility enactment towards patients indirectly through increased negative emotions towards patients and compassion fatigue.

issues.subcategory: Reverse causation not adequately tested
issues.description: Employees who are already fatigued or uncivil may perceive more patient incivility or elicit more negative patient reactions. Although the manuscript mentions stronger causal inference, it does not report cross-lagged or reciprocal models testing whether prior enacted incivility, fatigue, or emotions predict later experienced incivility.
issues.quote: This method also supports a lower likelihood of third variable effects ... and allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time.

issues.subcategory: Patient acuity operationalized as unvalidated single-item perception
issues.description: Patient acuity is defined as severity of illness and intensity of nursing care required, but it is measured by a single self-reported percentage of patients considered “severe,” based on unspecified and heterogeneous departmental scales. This conflates objective acuity, caseload composition, recall, subjective stress appraisal, and workload, and does not capture intensity of nursing care or number of patients.
issues.quote: we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were “severe.”

issues.subcategory: Heterogeneous acuity scales across departments and specialties
issues.description: The measure asks participants to use their department’s acuity scale but examples include ESI, CRIB, SOIS, and PRO tools, which are not equivalent and apply to different populations and settings. Percent severe is therefore not comparable across nurses or units. A nurse in an ICU and an ED may interpret “severe” very differently.
issues.quote: Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools

issues.subcategory: Experienced incivility source conflates patients and family/friends
issues.description: Experienced incivility is described as patient incivility but the measure includes patients and patient family members/friends. These sources may differ in frequency, power dynamics, emotional meaning, and implications for enacted incivility toward patients. Combining them weakens construct specificity.
issues.quote: how often have you been in a situation where any of your patients or patient family members/friends...

issues.subcategory: Outcome conflates incivility toward patients and families/friends
issues.description: Enacted incivility is described as incivility toward patients, but items include patients and patient family members. The hypothesized process implies incivility toward future patients, but the outcome may reflect behavior toward relatives or friends, which may have different antecedents and ethical implications.
issues.quote: Put down one or more patients/patient family members or acted condescendingly towards them

issues.subcategory: Shortened scales without full validation in target longitudinal context
issues.description: The authors selected only four items from incivility scales based on prior loadings and pilot correlations. Part-whole correlations with the full scale are inflated because the short scale is part of the full scale and do not establish content validity, longitudinal invariance, or equivalence after adapting “customer” to “patient.”
issues.quote: For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability... assessed part-whole correlations between the full scales and shortened versions during pilot testing

issues.subcategory: Negative emotions toward patients may overlap with compassion fatigue items
issues.description: Negative emotions include frustration, irritability, anger, and resentment toward patients. Compassion fatigue includes burnout symptoms such as irritability, aggression, cynicism, hopelessness, and trauma-related distress. Conceptual and item-content overlap likely contributes to extremely high correlations and challenges the proposed sequential mediation as distinct constructs.
issues.quote: The scale items consisted of four negative emotions: (a) frustration, (b) irritability, (c) anger, (d) resentment.

issues.subcategory: Compassion fatigue construct includes burnout and secondary trauma but modeled as unidimensional
issues.description: The manuscript defines compassion fatigue as consisting of burnout and secondary trauma components, yet uses a 13-item short scale apparently as a single score. Without reporting subscale structure, factor loadings, or whether the proposed mechanism differs by burnout versus secondary trauma, the operationalization may not match the conceptual definition.
issues.quote: Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components, with employees experiencing compassion fatigue if they are experiencing either caregiving-related burnout or secondary trauma (or both of these simultaneously).

issues.subcategory: Incivility enactment self-report vulnerable to social desirability and awareness limitations
issues.description: Enacted incivility is a socially undesirable behavior toward vulnerable patients. Self-report may underestimate or distort actual behavior, and employees may lack awareness of how patients perceive their actions. No social desirability controls or external reports are included.
issues.quote: Four items from the Enacted Incivility Scale (Cortina et al., 2001) were used to measure the frequency participants instigated incivility towards their patients.

issues.subcategory: Misattribution of stressor-emotion model to social learning theory
issues.description: The manuscript states it utilizes social learning theory, then immediately describes the stressor-emotion model of CWB. These are distinct frameworks. Social learning theory concerns observational learning/modeling, whereas the hypothesized mediation is stressor-emotion-fatigue-CWB. The theory section conflates frameworks and does not develop actual social learning mechanisms.
issues.quote: To understand how incivility experiences from customers may be impacting employee affect and behavior over time, we utilize social learning theory (Bandura, 1977). This model considers how individuals learn behaviors through observation and modeling of others' actions and their consequences, ultimately shaping counterproductive work behaviors (CWB), such as enacted incivility. Applied to enacted incivility, the general premise of the model suggests that enacted incivility occurs due to a sequence of events where environmental stressors at work lead to enacted incivility through appraisal, perceptions of the stressor, and negative emotions (Spector & Fox, 2005).

issues.subcategory: Customer-service analogy for nurse-patient relationship underdeveloped
issues.description: The manuscript treats patients and families as customers and nurses as service employees, but nurse-patient relationships include clinical duty, vulnerability, care ethics, institutional constraints, and asymmetrical expertise. The authors acknowledge complexity but still generalize customer incivility frameworks without fully addressing whether customer reciprocity and CWB constructs apply equivalently in healthcare.
issues.quote: We view the patient-nurse relationship as a specialized form of customer-employee relationship. However, it is important to understand that this relationship includes care provision and care coordination, which is more complex and dynamic than some other employee-customer relationships.

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis 2 text has grammatical and conceptual ambiguity
issues.description: Hypothesis 2 states “higher levels of experienced patient incivility is associated with increased compassion fatigue,” and describes an indirect association but does not specify temporal ordering in the hypothesis itself. This is minor grammatically but reflects broader ambiguity in whether the claim is longitudinal change or between-person association.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 2:  Experienced patient incivility is positively and indirectly related to compassion fatigue through negative emotions towards patients: higher levels of experienced patient incivility is associated with increased compassion fatigue due to increased negative emotions towards patients.

issues.subcategory: Coworker incivility mentioned instead of patient/customer incivility
issues.description: The compassion fatigue section says the study examines experiencing coworker incivility, contradicting the study’s focus on patient/customer incivility. This appears to be a substantive editing error that could confuse the construct being tested.
issues.quote: Within the current study, we look specifically at the relationship between experiencing coworker incivility and experiencing a caregiving specific form of job burnout, compassion fatigue.

issues.subcategory: Title says customers but model and measures use patients and families
issues.description: The title frames the study as incivility with customers, while the sample and measures are specifically nurses interacting with patients and families. This is not merely wording; patients are not equivalent to customers in important theoretical and practical respects.
issues.quote: Incivility begets incivility: Understanding the relationship between experienced and enacted incivility with customers over time

issues.subcategory: Retention rate reporting inconsistent with stated counts
issues.description: The manuscript reports 98% retention at each interval, but 458/468=97.9%, 454/458=99.1%, and 450/454=99.1%. Rounding all to 98% is imprecise and obscures the true pattern. More importantly, because nonrespondents were dropped from later invitations, these are conditional response rates rather than true retention opportunities.
issues.quote: n = 468 nurses responded at time 1; n = 458 responded at time 2 (98% retention rate between T1 and T2); n = 454 responded at time 3 (98% retention rate between T2 and T3); and n = 450 responded at time 4 (98% retention rate between T3 and T4).

issues.subcategory: No preregistration or analysis plan reported
issues.description: The study includes multiple waves, several possible time-lag choices, controls, moderated mediation, supplemental analyses, scale shortening, and exclusion criteria. No preregistration, registered hypotheses, or analysis plan is reported, leaving substantial researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: We tested our hypotheses using data collected across four waves separated by one-week lags.

issues.subcategory: Selective use of waves despite measuring all variables every wave
issues.description: All variables were measured at every wave, but the reported model uses T2 incivility, T3 negative emotions, and T4 compassion fatigue/enacted incivility. The rationale for excluding parallel models using other adjacent waves or aggregating all lags is insufficient. Different wave selections could yield different results.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks. ... Figure 1 for information what measurement period each variable in the model was taken from

issues.subcategory: Unclear control variable selection
issues.description: Tables include work hours at T2/T3 and the title references T1 controls, but the methods do not justify why work hours were controlled, whether other demographics or baseline constructs were considered, or how controls were selected. Unspecified control selection can materially affect mediation estimates.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents intercorrelations among study variables and descriptive information.

issues.subcategory: Post hoc supplemental analyses not clearly distinguished from planned analyses
issues.description: The manuscript conducts supplemental analyses on unhypothesized moderation and relative importance but does not clarify whether they were exploratory, corrected for multiple testing, or preplanned. These analyses are interpreted substantively despite being underreported and internally inconsistent.
issues.quote: Supplemental analyses. We conducted a series of supplemental analyses to 1) address unhypothesized moderation effects and 2) investigate the relationship between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility.

issues.subcategory: Insufficient details on data quality exclusions
issues.description: The authors mention a priori data quality checks but do not provide the full set of criteria, thresholds for “reasonably consistent” demographics, whether exclusions were blind to outcomes, or the missing 21 poor-quality exclusion reasons. This affects reproducibility and bias assessment.
issues.quote: Responses were considered failed data quality checks if they had any of the following characteristics: (a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age); or (b) missing values exceeded 50% of the questions (n = 1).

issues.subcategory: No power analysis
issues.description: No a priori power analysis or minimum detectable effect is reported. This is especially important for moderated mediation and interaction effects, which require larger samples, and for Table 3 where the sample is reduced to N=244 due to missing moderator data.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.subcategory: No details on centering or scaling of interaction variables
issues.description: The interaction between customer incivility and patient acuity is reported, but the manuscript does not state whether variables were mean-centered, standardized, or left raw. This affects interpretation of main effects and simple slopes, particularly because patient acuity is a proportion and incivility is a Likert mean.
issues.quote: Results revealed that the Time 2 experienced incivility × Time 2 perceived patient acuity interaction term was significant (B = .34, SE = .12, p < .01).

issues.subcategory: No measurement invariance across time
issues.description: The study makes longitudinal claims and administers identical measures across waves, but does not test whether constructs have comparable measurement properties over time. Without longitudinal measurement invariance, changes or lagged relations may reflect shifts in interpretation or measurement artifacts.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.subcategory: Incomplete reporting of alternative CFA models
issues.description: The manuscript states the hypothesized model fit better than alternatives but does not report the alternative model specifications, fit indices, chi-square difference tests, or factor correlations. This prevents evaluation of discriminant validity.
issues.quote: and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors.

issues.subcategory: No information on hospitals, units, or clustering
issues.description: Participants came from various hospitals across the U.S., but the number of hospitals/units represented, clustering by facility/unit, and whether multiple respondents came from the same workplace are not reported. Unit-level culture and patient population could confound results, and clustering could affect standard errors.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies.

issues.subcategory: Potential nonindependence ignored
issues.description: If multiple nurses were recruited from the same hospitals, units, or professional networks, responses may not be independent. Shared unit climate, patient acuity, management, and staffing could induce clustering. The analyses appear to treat all observations as independent.
issues.quote: First, we dropped off recruitment flyers with the study information at three hospitals local to the research team.

issues.subcategory: No response rate or denominator
issues.description: The authors state the full population sampled from is unknown and recruitment was open via flyers and online postings. Without a denominator or response rate, it is impossible to assess selection bias.
issues.quote: Although the full population size that was sampled from is unknown

issues.subcategory: Demographic reporting incomplete for sample evaluation
issues.description: The manuscript reports gender, age, race/ethnicity, and tenure, but omits key nursing variables such as unit type, role/licensure, shift length, shift type, number of patients, region, hospital type, full-time status distribution, and years in nursing. These are important for interpreting acuity, incivility exposure, and generalizability.
issues.quote: The majority of respondents were female (96.64%), with a mean age of 34.44 (SD = 5.49) years.

issues.subcategory: Overgeneralization from nurses to service employees/customers
issues.description: The sample is nurses in high-stakes healthcare settings, yet the discussion generalizes to service employees and customer service broadly. Healthcare interactions differ substantially from retail, hospitality, and other service settings, and the sample is overwhelmingly female and self-selected.
issues.quote: Using a four-wave data collection of service employees within the healthcare industry, we examined how and why experiencing incivility from patients is related to future enactment of incivility towards patients.

issues.subcategory: Limited representativeness of gender composition
issues.description: The sample is 96.64% female, higher than the cited 88% of registered nurses. While nursing is female-dominated, this distribution limits conclusions about male nurses or more gender-diverse healthcare teams, especially because incivility experiences and enactment may differ by gender.
issues.quote: The majority of respondents were female (96.64%)

issues.subcategory: Unknown applicability outside high-acuity settings
issues.description: The target population is high-stakes/critical care settings where incivility, stress, and patient acuity may be unusually high. Results should not be generalized to lower-acuity nursing, outpatient care, long-term care, or nonclinical service roles without replication.
issues.quote: The target population of this research included nurses within healthcare industries, particularly those working in high-stakes or critical care settings.

issues.subcategory: Practice recommendations imply intervention targets without causal evidence
issues.description: The manuscript recommends identifying employees experiencing incivility and intervening to stop downstream affective and behavioral processes. While plausible, the observational design cannot establish that reducing experienced incivility or providing supports would reduce enacted incivility through the proposed mediators.
issues.quote: Organizations should identify who is experiencing high levels of incivility and develop support systems and interventions for these employees to stop the negative affective and energetic process our results suggest are occurring.

issues.subcategory: Same-time mediator and outcome in final mediation stage
issues.description: Compassion fatigue and enacted incivility are both measured at T4 in the mediation model. This undermines the temporal ordering required for the final causal path from compassion fatigue to enacted incivility and makes the serial mediation only partially longitudinal. The model cannot determine whether compassion fatigue precedes enacted incivility, enacted incivility precedes fatigue, or both reflect concurrent distress.
issues.quote: T4 Compassion Fatigue ... T4 Enacted Incivility

issues.subcategory: Temporal lag justification insufficient and generic
issues.description: The authors assert that one-week lags are sufficient and effects will not meaningfully differ from longer lags, but no construct-specific rationale is provided for incivility → emotion → compassion fatigue → enacted incivility. Compassion fatigue may develop over longer periods, whereas emotions may fluctuate within shifts. Lag mismatch can bias longitudinal mediation.
issues.quote: Previous studies have shown that lags spanning this length of time are sufficient for observing emergence of such counterproductive behaviors as incivility and that the observed effects will not meaningfully differ from studies featuring longer periods of time between waves

issues.subcategory: Weekly recall may not capture event-based incivility accurately
issues.description: The study argues for cumulative weekly exposure, but participants retrospectively report frequency over the past week. Recall may be biased by mood, salience, shift schedule, number of shifts, and recent events. Work hours are included inconsistently but number of shifts and patient contacts are not incorporated.
issues.quote: For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.

issues.subcategory: Exposure not adjusted for patient-contact opportunity
issues.description: Experienced and enacted incivility frequencies depend on number of shifts, hours worked, number of patients, patient turnover, and family contact. The study measures work hours but does not consistently adjust for patient volume or contact opportunities, making comparisons across nurses problematic.
issues.quote: worked more than one shift a week, on average, and routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients.

issues.subcategory: Monte Carlo procedure underreported
issues.description: The manuscript reports using 20,000 Monte Carlo replications but does not specify whether estimates came from observed-variable regressions, SEM, standardized or unstandardized coefficients, covariance matrices used, or whether nonnormality and missing data were handled. This limits reproducibility.
issues.quote: We then used a Monte Carlo simulation with 20,000 replications (Zyphur et al., 2016) to construct confidence intervals around the parameter estimates of all indirect effects and the Index of Moderated Mediation (IMM).
